newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD - FOOD, TECHNICALS TO HIKE AUG CPI.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD - FOOD, TECHNICALS TO HIKE AUG CPI.

text.p: A strong increase in food prices combined with technical factors should push South African year-on-year consumer price inflation sharply higher in August, economists polled by Reuters said.

The consensus forecast for the figure, due on Thursday at 0900 GMT, was 7.7 percent from 7.1 percent in July, when consumer inflation rose above seven percent for the first time since August last year.
The range for the year-on-year figure was put at between 7.6 and 7.9 percent, while the month-on-month rate of increase was seen little changed at 0.7 percent from 0.8 percent in July.
Economists said further upward pressure on inflation, which began with a 1.0 percentage point increase in June, would come from a substantial increase in the the food component of the index.

Vegetable and fruit prices in particular were expected to have risen sharply following the cold weather experienced by the country in July, while Sanlam economist Pieter Calitz said he also expected meat prices to rise sharply in the month.
A low base figure in August 1995 was also seen contributing as was the feeding through of price pressures due to the rand's sharp plunge since mid-February.
Nick Barnardt, economist at BOE Natwest, said inflation would push higher throughout the next few months, driven by food price pressure and the effects of the currency decline.
"Food inflation will be on an up-trend from now on...also one must allow for the possibility of the rand depreciation to come through," he said.

Rand Merchant Bank treasury economist Julia Roy noted that an unfavourable base effect would probably be very obvious in the food component of the index due to a 1.2 percent month-on-month decline in the food index in August 1995.
Looking ahead, economists expected a year-on-year figure firmly above eight percent in September, rising towards nine percent by year-end.
"We expect a rising trend over the remaining month towards nine percent at year-end," Roy said.
Internationally, debt supply and Europe's finances will provide the main focus for financial markets in the week ahead, analysts said.
An informal meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin, details of the French budget for 1997 and debt auctions in various European countries are among the week's highlights.

In the U.S., bond supply will also be a concern and markets will be looking at some of the final economic data releases in the week running up to the meeting of the Federal Reserve Open Market Committee (FOMC) on September 24.
In the U.S., August capacity utilisation and industrial production data are due on Tuesday.
U.S. July international trade figures will follow on Wednesday and Thursday will see the release of August housing starts and the September Philadelphia Fed Index.
Analysts said all the U.S. data would be watched closely as the FOMC approached.
The U.S. Treasury will detail its auction of two- and five-year notes on Wednesday. The auctions will be held the following week on September 24 and 25 respectively.
The Bundesbank is due to meet on Thursday, but analysts did not expect any change in the repo rate.
